title: DFS in Zürich: One Deep Dive to the Destination
description: Watch DFS explore Zürich’s street grid by going as deep as possible before backtracking. This visualization shows how traversal order reshapes the path found on a real-world-style map graph.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ DFS in Zürich (Seefeld) — going deep before you go back. 🌉

In Depth-First Search (DFS), we treat the street map as a graph: intersections become nodes and road segments become edges. 🕸️ Starting from a source node, DFS follows one neighbor path all the way down (deep recursion/stack), marking visited nodes to prevent cycles, then backtracks when it hits a dead end. 🔁

On a real street-map-inspired grid, that means DFS may not produce the shortest route—but it reveals a deterministic “route discovery” pattern based on neighbor ordering. 📍🧠 The key idea: DFS is about reachability and traversal structure, not shortest distance (that’s where BFS/Dijkstra shine). 

Want the next reel for BFS vs DFS on the same Zürich map? Comment your pick and hit follow! 🚀
fb_caption:
🗺️ Zürich (Seefeld) street maps, visualized with DFS (Depth-First Search)! 

In graph search terms, DFS explores as far as possible along a path before backtracking, using a stack/recursion and a visited set to avoid loops. ✅ By modeling intersections as nodes and streets as edges, we can see how traversal order changes what gets explored first—great for teaching graph theory and search mechanics.
